[{"ghsa_id":"GHSA-859w-52fx-hcm6","cve_id":"CVE-2026-64855","url":"https://api.github.com/advisories/GHSA-859w-52fx-hcm6","html_url":"https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-859w-52fx-hcm6","summary":"soapbar: verify_envelope_bsp accepts an unauthenticated embedded certificate (signature forgery / authentication bypass)","description":"### Impact `verify_envelope_bsp()` derived its trust anchor from the message it was verifying. It read the X.509 certificate out of the caller-untrusted `wsse:BinarySecurityToken`, validated **only** that certificate's not-before / not-after dates, and then verified the signature against that same certificate. There was no CA-chain validation, no issuer/subject allowlist, and no pinning. A successful `verify_envelope_bsp()` therefore proved only that the envelope was signed by *whoever supplied the embedded certificate* — never that it was signed by a *trusted* party. An attacker who mints their own certificate, signs a forged envelope, and embeds that certificate in the token passes verification. Any consumer that treats a successful BSP verification as authentication can be impersonated (signature forgery / authentication bypass). `verify_envelope()` (which pins a caller-supplied `x509_cert`) was **not** affected — the flaw was specific to the BSP variant whose trust anchor came from the message. ### Affected versions soapbar `< 0.13.0` (all published versions exposing `verify_envelope_bsp`). ### Patches Fixed in **0.13.0**. `verify_envelope_bsp` now fails closed unless the caller anchors trust: - `trusted_certs=[...]` — pin the expected signer certificate(s); the embedded certificate must equal one of them. - `ca_certs=[...]` — accept certificates directly issued by trusted CA(s). With neither supplied, verification raises instead of trusting the message's own certificate. The trust anchor is checked before the signature is relied upon. `verify_cert_trust=False` restores the old (insecure) behaviour explicitly. ### Workarounds Before upgrading: - Do not treat a successful `verify_envelope_bsp()` as authentication. - Prefer `verify_envelope(..., x509_cert=)`, which pins the expected certificate. - If BSP is required, validate the embedded certificate against your own trust store before acting on the verification Polynomial-time ReDoS when matching untrusted names against multi-star patterns (default flags)","description":"# Summary With default flags, a pattern that contains several `*` wildcards takes polynomial time, O(n^k) for k stars, to reject a crafted file name. The pattern is an ordinary developer constant such as `*_*_*_*_*.csv`; only the string being matched comes from the attacker. A 255-byte file name (the maximum on common filesystems) takes 73 s with `fnmatch.fnmatch()` and 86 s with `glob.globmatch()`. The standard library's `fnmatch` handles the same input in under a millisecond. This is different from GHSA-84v8-qmgq-9g88: that advisory covers extglob patterns, while this case needs no flags and no attacker-controlled pattern. # Details Every `*` is translated to a lazy `.*?` (`_STAR`, `wcmatch/_wcparse.py:212`; `_PATH_STAR` `[^/]*?`, `:218`), which is emitted in `_handle_star` (`:1405-1424`): ```text *_*_*_*_*.csv -> ^(?s:(?=.)(?![.]).*?_.*?_.*?_.*?_.*?\.csv)$ ``` When the subject consists of many `_` and does not end in `.csv`, the regex engine tries every way of splitting it between the stars. CPython fixed the same problem in its own `fnmatch` (bpo-40480) by making every star segment except the last one atomic. # PoC ```python import time, fnmatch as std from wcmatch import fnmatch, glob for pat, n in [('*_*_*_*.csv', 255), ('*_*_*_*.csv', 400), ('*_*_*_*_*.csv', 150), ('*_*_*_*_*.csv', 200), ('*_*_*_*_*.csv', 255)]: name = '_' * n t = time.perf_counter(); fnmatch.fnmatch(name, pat); w = time.perf_counter() - t t = time.perf_counter(); std.fnmatchcase(name, pat); s = time.perf_counter() - t print(f'{pat:15} len={n} wcmatch={w:.3f}s stdlib={s:.5f}s') t = time.perf_counter(); glob.globmatch('uploads/' + '_' * 255, 'uploads/*_*_*_*_*.csv') print(f'globmatch {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s') ``` wcmatch 11.1, CPython 3.13, macOS: ```text *_*_*_*.csv len=255 wcmatch=1.412s stdlib=0.00001s *_*_*_*.csv len=400 wcmatch=8.599s stdlib=0.00004s *_*_*_*_*.csv len=150 wcmatch=5.333s stdlib=0.00003s *_*_*_*_*.csv len=200 wcmatch=22.415s stdlib=0.00007s *_*_*_*_*.csv len=255 wcmatch=72.732s stdlib=0.00047s globmatch 85.75s ``` `glob.glob('*_*_*_*.csv', root_dir=d)` on a real directory that contains one file named `'_' * 255` takes 1.7 s. # Impact Applications that match untrusted names against multi-star patterns can be blocked on a single CPU core for minutes per name. Examples: upload handlers, archive or object-store key filters, and `glob`/`WcMatch` scans of directories where other users can create files. No authentication is needed. # Fix Emit every star segment except the last one as an atomic group, as the standard library does. On Python 3.11 and later use `(?>.*?_)`; on 3.10 use the lookahead/backreference form from `fnmatch._join_translated_parts`. For example: ```text ^(?s:(?=.)(?![.])(?>.*?_)(?>.*?_)(?>.*?_)(?>.*?_).*?\.csv)$ ``` This rejects the 255-byte name in under 1 ms. On my spot-check inputs it gives the same results as the current regex. The same change applies to Quadratic memory growth from sibling elements in get_text()","description":"# Summary Every sibling `
` adds another level of the parent's indentation, so the size of `get_text()` output grows quadratically with the number of tables. In the measurements below, a 240 KB HTML document produces about 1 billion characters and uses about 1 GB of memory. # Details `table_end_handler()` (`model/tag/table_tag.py`) writes the rendered table into the parent element with `HtmlElement.write_verbatim_text()` (`model/html_element.py`). For a block-level parent, `write_verbatim_text()` calls `canvas.open_block()`, which pushes the parent's `padding_inline` onto the prefix stack. The following `close_block()` never pops it; only `Canvas.close_tag()` calls `prefix.remove_last_prefix()`. So each table leaves one extra padding entry on the stack. This has been present since 2.0 (commit 84ec720). ```python >>> get_text('
    ' + '
a
' * 4 + '') ' a\n \n a\n \n a\n \n a\n ' ``` # PoC ```python import sys, time, resource from inscriptis import get_text n = int(sys.argv[1]) html = "
    " + "
    " * n + "
" t = time.time(); out = get_text(html) print(len(html), f"{time.time()-t:.2f}s", len(out), resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss // 2**20, "MiB") ``` inscriptis 2.7.5, Python 3.11, macOS (2.0.0 behaves the same): | tables | HTML | time | output chars | peak RSS | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1,000 | 15 KB | 0.02 s | 4.0 M | 31 MiB | | 4,000 | 60 KB | 0.33 s | 64 M | 154 MiB | | 8,000 | 120 KB | 1.31 s | 256 M | 463 MiB | | 16,000 | 240 KB | 5.63 s | 1,024 M | 991 MiB | When the input doubles, output size and memory grow about 4 times. # Impact Any application that converts untrusted HTML with inscriptis can be made to exhaust memory with a small document. This includes crawlers, RAG and LLM ingestion pipelines, and `inscriptis-api`. No authentication and no user interaction are needed. # Fix ```diff self.canvas.write(self, text, whitespace=WhiteSpace.pre) if self.display == Display.block: + self.canvas.current_block.prefix.remove_last_prefix() self.canvas.close_block(self) ``` With this change the 240 KB input above produces 288 K characters in 0.14 s with 27 MiB peak RSS. A single table renders exactly as before, and the existing test suite
